To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Escherichia Coli cell cycle has a highly variable duration, that it is controlled by a homeostatic mechanism and that the cell cycle duration is determined by the time between cell division and cell birth.

1) the cell cycle of E. coli can be described in terms of a sequence of cell-cycle intervals defined by key molecular processes, 2) these intervals are highly correlated with each other in a reproducible manner in many individual cells, 3) these correlations are not due to cell-to-cell variability, but to inherent cell-cycle variability that affects all cells, and 4) this cell-cycle variability has an underlying homeostatic control.
the cell cycle of E. coli can be quantified by a step by step, cell by cell approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantitative description and understanding of cell-cycle regulation.
the development of a new approach to the study of the cell cycle, which will be based on the analysis of single cell data.
a better understanding of the bacterial cell cycle, and with developing new methods for the study of single cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bacterial cell cycle is not a simple deterministic process but a highly regulated stochastic process.
the bacterial cell cycle is a complex, but well-ordered and highly controlled process.
the bacterial cell cycle is not a clockwork but a stochastic machine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
single-cell data are changing our view on the cell cycle.
we are still missing the single-cell view of the cell cycle.
we have shown that single-cell measurements of cell-cycle events are feasible, and have provided a method for their analysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to move from a population-centric to a single-cell-centric view of the bacterial cell cycle.

the cell cycle is not a rigidly programmed sequence of events but rather an adaptive and dynamic process that can be understood in terms of a set of homeostatic controls that are coordinated to achieve the cell division rate and the size of the cell.
the cell cycle is not a simple deterministic machine.
